questions.q: What are the three parts of the Arrange / Act / Assert pattern, in order?
options: Set up data, call the method under test, check the result
questions.explain: Arrange builds the data/inputs the test needs, Act calls the single method under test, and Assert checks that the outcome matches expectations.

questions.q: A developer writes one giant @isTest method that inserts records, calls a method, asserts, then inserts different records, calls the method again, and asserts again. What's the main problem with this?
options: Apex does not allow more than one assertion per test method
It will always fail code coverage requirements
When one of the scenarios fails, the method name alone won't tell you which scenario broke
Test methods are not allowed to contain more than one insert statement
questions.explain: Splitting distinct behaviors into separate, well-named test methods means a failure immediately tells you which specific claim about the code broke.

questions.q: Which method name best follows the naming convention described in this lesson?
questions.explain: A good test method name describes the scenario and the expected outcome, so a failing test is understandable from its name alone — testMethod1 and doTest convey nothing.

questions.q: Why should test methods be written to be independent of one another?
options: Because each @isTest method runs with its own fresh transaction and rolled-back data, and relying on another test's leftover data would be fragile and order-dependent
Because Apex runs all test methods in a class simultaneously on different threads
Because Salesforce deletes the entire org's data after each test method
Independence doesn't matter in Apex test classes
questions.explain: Since data created in one test method is rolled back when that method ends, a test that depended on another test's data would fail unpredictably depending on execution order.

questions.q: By convention in this course, what should a test class covering OpportunityService be named?
questions.explain: The convention shown in this lesson is `<ClassName>Test` — e.g. OpportunityServiceTest for a class named OpportunityService.
